title: Cells No Guard Can See
statement:
A floor plan is an m × n grid. Some cells hold a guard (guards[i] = [row, col]) and some hold a wall (walls[j] = [row, col]). All these positions are distinct.

A guard looks straight up, down, left and right. The line of sight continues cell by cell until it reaches the edge of the grid, a wall, or another guard; those block it.

Return how many cells are empty (no guard, no wall) and not seen by any guard.

examples.why: The guard at (0, 0) sees (0, 1) before the wall, and (1, 0), (2, 0) below. The guard at (2, 3) sees its whole row and column. Only (1, 2) is left: the walls cut off every line toward it.
The guard sees (0, 0) and (0, 2). The wall hides (0, 4) and (0, 5).
The guards block each other vertically, but between them they cover the top two rows and (2, 1). The corners (2, 0) and (2, 2) stay unseen.

constraints: All positions are distinct and inside the grid
hints: Mark guards and walls on a grid. Walking every guard's four lines works, but a long empty row with many guards gets walked again and again.
Think about one row, scanned left to right. A cell is seen from the left if the last guard or wall you passed was a guard.

Sweep every row left→right and right→left, and every column top→bottom and bottom→top, carrying a "guard in view" flag that turns on at a guard and off at a wall. Mark seen cells, then count empty unmarked ones.

explain.intuition:
Seeing from the left is a property you can carry while scanning. Walk a row from left to right with a flag watching. A guard turns it on, a wall turns it off, and every empty cell you pass while it is on is seen. Another guard simply turns it on again, which already models "guards block each other": the cells after it are seen anyway, by the new guard.

Do the same sweep in all four directions. Each sweep touches every cell once, so the whole job is linear in the grid size, no matter how many guards there are. Walking each guard's lines individually can also be fast if you stop as soon as you reach a cell already seen from the same direction, but the sweep is simpler to get right.
steps: Build a grid: 0 empty, 1 guard, 2 wall, and a separate seen grid.
For each row, sweep left to right and right to left. Set watching to true at a guard, false at a wall, and mark empty cells as seen while it is true.
Do the same for each column, top to bottom and bottom to top.
Count cells that are empty and not marked seen.
pitfalls: Walking each guard's lines all the way to a wall or edge, ignoring guards in the way. The answer stays right, because the blocked cells are seen by the other guard, but a row full of guards is then walked once per guard, which is quadratic.
Counting guard or wall cells as unseen. Only empty cells count.
Mixing up rows and columns on a non-square grid. With a flat array the index is row · n + col, where n is the number of columns.

solutions.title: Look out from every empty cell
solutions.idea: For each empty cell, walk in all four directions until something blocks. If the first thing met is a guard, the cell is seen.

solutions.title: Four sweeps with a watching flag
solutions.idea: Sweep each row and column in both directions. A guard switches the flag on, a wall switches it off, and empty cells passed while it is on are seen.

followups: Guards can now see diagonally as well. What extra sweeps do you need?
Walls are added one at a time and you must report the count after each. Can you update only the affected row and column?
